cards.tag: Adds: a stated number Jev passed over
cards.title: Finds the probability the person actually gave
cards.quote: Roughly 70% for AI takeover or a comparably permanent catastrophe—not specifically human extinction.
cards.body: Today the engine shows an inferred ≈78% here; Jev passed over this sentence. Clairic proposed it, Jev’s check accepted it, and the result shows his stated 70%, which matches his public statement.

cards.title: Turns timing into a year
cards.quote: My rough forecast is full AI-research automation around 2030–31, with systems outperforming humans across essentially all jobs around a 2033 median, though those dates are quite uncertain…
cards.body: Clairic reads 2033 for work, and resolves relative timing against the interview date (Elon Musk’s “within ten years” becomes 2036). Today’s page shows only the quote. Six featured timelines gained a year; one is wrong (David Sacks’ “over the next several years” became 2026), so years need the same review as the rest of a simulated profile.

cards.title: Reads “approximately zero” as a stated value
cards.body: Today’s engine only picks up digits with a percent sign, so this showed as an inferred <1%. With Clairic it is read as stated, and Jev’s check accepts it. Odds in words are rare: about 6 of 1,297 production participants gave them without a digit.

cards.title: Says zero when no number was given
cards.quote: I don’t think a precise percentage would be honest or useful.
cards.body: With a plain number field, Clairic returned 0% for Altman, Gary Marcus and Eliezer Yudkowsky, none of whom gave a number. A strict “null, not zero” rule fixed all of them, but it shows why every find needs a check.

cards.title: Takes old or conditional estimates at face value
cards.quote: I previously said 10–20% seemed reasonable, but that was a gut feeling, not a calibrated estimate…
cards.body: Clairic proposed 10% here, and 90% from Max Tegmark’s “over 90% for humanity losing control if we continue deploying superintelligence without effective predeployment safety regulation.” Jev’s check rejected both, as it does today.

cards.title: Letting Clairic choose the quotes lost some
cards.who: The whole span Clairic returned for Bill Gates
cards.body: Clairic returns the smallest span, so code widens it to the sentence. Even then, when Clairic picked the quotes instead of Jev, simulated-user pages showed 14 timelines instead of 22 and 90 assumption and update quotes instead of 100. Jev keeps that job in the recommended setup.

recs.title: Keep Jev as the engine for interviews and results
recs.body: Clef runs our engine unchanged, but it reads people differently: 28 of 47 featured users move more than 0.1 on the map, further from the reference readings; P(doom) falls within 2× of the references for 19% of people instead of 72%; and it picks a different next question about a third of the time. It is also about 7× slower and 5× more expensive. Our questions were tuned on Jev for months, so some of that gap is tuning, but closing it would be a re-tuning project, not a swap.

recs.title: Don’t add Clairic to the participant interview yet
recs.body: For real participants it could only change the stated P(doom), and the gain is small: about 6 of 1,297 production participants gave odds in words without a digit, and Jev already reads typed percentages. It would add 18% to model spend, about 0.3 s to each result, and a dependency on a preview model.

recs.title: Optionally use Clairic as an add-on in simulated-user generation
recs.body: With Jev still choosing every quote, all 47 featured results kept today’s findings and quotes. Clairic added two stated P(doom) values Jev had passed over (Kokotajlo, McAfee) and a year on six timelines, for about $0.004 more per simulated user. Generation runs offline and is reviewed before publishing, so the preview risk is low. Showing the year needs a small UI change on simulated-user pages.

recs.title: Use Clairic to find values, never to estimate them
recs.body: Its estimates of an unstated P(doom) and of map positions pull everyone toward the middle of the scale and were clearly worse than Jev’s. Keep Jev’s likelihood bands and the map ladder. If Clairic is used, every value it finds goes through a Jev check and a few code rules (no zero for a missing number, no past or unwritten years).

recs.title: Re-run this comparison when Clef leaves preview
recs.body: Both Cloudflare models are early checkpoints. The harness replays all featured users through each setup in about 10 minutes for about $5. The Clef adapter could also serve as an emergency fallback if TypeSafe is unavailable, accepting that results would read noticeably differently.
